title: Being a good friend
hookLine: a friendship quiz, and the seven marks of a friend (AN 7.36)
tomorrow: why did the Buddha once walk off alone into an elephant's forest?

cards: Online friendship quizzes ask the easy things: their favorite color, their go-to order, their middle name. The Buddha's quiz is harder.
In a short teaching in the Anguttara Nikaya, he names seven marks of a friend worth keeping. A friend gives what's hard to give. Does what's hard to do.
Bears what's hard to bear. Tells you their secrets. Keeps yours.
Doesn't leave you in trouble. And doesn't look down on you when you're down. Read it as a mirror, not a scorecard.

teach.b: Notice where the weight falls. Three of the seven start with hard: hard to give, hard to do, hard to bear. Friendship, here, is measured in the moments it costs something.
Two marks are about trust running both ways: telling your secrets, and keeping theirs. A friend lets you see them, and guards what you have shown.
And the last two are about the bad stretch: not leaving, and not looking down. That's the friend in need.
Now this week, all of it, one line at a time. When love ends, the bond can stop, and the wish for their good can stay: kind at the end. Parents care by steering: guide them.
Rahula's mirror, before, during and after: reflect first. Ryokan in the field all night: play. Kisa Gotami at every door: held gently.
Four good-hearted friends, and a direction to steer by: north.

Put them side by side and they make one picture of a person: someone who wishes well even at a distance, steers gently, looks before acting, plays with their whole heart, stays near grief, and shows up when it's hard.
That's a good friend too. None of it needs a grand gesture. It fits inside an ordinary Tuesday.

how: Buddhist teachers sometimes read the seven marks of a friend from the Anguttara Nikaya alongside the Sigalovada, as a way to look at the kind of friend one is.

games.q: what does “being a good friend” mean?
o: being easy company and never asking for anything
agreeing with a friend so the mood stays light
showing up in the moments a friendship costs something

games.q: seven marks, one week — tap the pairs.

s: the seven marks of a friend are mostly about having fun together
three start with hard: hard to give, hard to do, hard to bear.
the list includes not looking down on you when you're down
the last two marks are about the bad stretch: not leaving and not looking down.

games.q: a friend got cut from the team and is avoiding everyone. you're slammed this week. which mark of a friend fits best?
o: give them space; true friends wait to be asked before reaching out.
send a long text with advice on how to make the team next year.
show up for ten minutes: don't leave, and don't look down on them.
games.why: the last two marks are exactly this: not leaving in trouble, and not looking down when someone's down.

practice: Go back over the seven marks slowly, one breath for each. When one catches, the one that feels hardest, stay there. Bring to mind a friend who needs exactly that from you right now, and picture one small, real way to give it.
If no one comes to mind, rest on someone who has been that friend for you.

wordCard.voice: Being a good friend: the seven marks turned toward yourself, weighed in the moments that cost something.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: be the friend in need, on the hard day especially. Two of six, with a week behind you.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 7.36 (Mitta Sutta: a friend gives what is hard to give, does what is hard to do, endures what is hard to endure, reveals his secrets, keeps your secrets, does not abandon you in misfortune, does not despise you when you are down)
